items.title: Ukraine's Secret Weapon: The Points System Winning the Drone War | Andrii Hrytseniuk
items.summary: Ukraine tracks every confirmed drone kill with video evidence, deduplicates the data to prevent double-counting, converts verified strikes into e-points, and delivers newly ordered weapons to frontline units in two weeks instead of twelve months. Andrii Hrytseniuk, CEO of Brave1- Ukraine's government defense innovation agency - joins Craig Smith to explain in precise operational detail how what started as a consumer loyalty program concept became the most consequential military procurement reform in modern warfare. The Army of Drones Bonus Program, running on the Delta command ecosystem with AI-assisted verification and a marketplace built like a military Amazon, has produced outcomes nobody predicted at launch: 35,000 Russian casualties per month confirmed with video evidence, the ability to change military targeting priorities instantly across an entire army by adjusting point values, and the identification of unknown high-performing frontline units whose methods are now being replicated across the force. The conversation reveals details that rarely surface in coverage of the conflict. Capturing Russian soldiers earns more bonus points than killing them, a deliberate design choice reflecting the preference not to kill when alternatives exist, and drones are actively being used to guide surrendering Russian soldiers to Ukrainian positions. The Delta ecosystem contains the world's largest military AI training dataset, already being used by defense companies to train targeting, interception, and recognition models. And perhaps most significantly: the US and France are now implementing similar marketplace and decentralized procurement approaches modeled directly on what Brave1 demonstrated works at scale. Ukraine is no longer just a recipient of military support. It is the primary laboratory for the future of warfare, and it is actively exporting what it has learned. items.title: Interview #94 Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM, Splunk at Cisco
items.summary: Kamal Hathi, SVP and GM of Splunk at Cisco, breaks down why intent is never enough to control an AI agent: agents are ruthless goal seekers, and asking one to free up 3 percent of disk space can end with 97 percent free because nobody said keep the rest. He explains why trust means verification rather than instruction, and why it includes the invoice, comparing it to hiring a contractor you trust to build a house that stands without emptying your bank account. Kamal also digs into why the rush toward air gapped and local AI is driven less by distrust of frontier labs than by cost, with specialized small models running 97 percent cheaper and 95 percent faster than frontier calls, and why the real threat is the unknown unknowns, agents nobody cataloged acting inside a state of perpetual breach. Finally, he argues agents are the new apps, and every job starts to look like a software developer's: tell the agent what to do, inspect the work, and iterate.
